## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Large Language Models
  Code                    CSC_53432_EP
  Team and workload       Instructor: Guokan Shang (MBZUAI) · 24 h · 2 ECTS · theory + labs on LLM development and deployment: tokenization, architecture, pre-training and scaling laws, post-training (SFT, RLHF, DPO, GRPO), inference, RAG, agents, multimodality, evaluation and safety — and Shang's research.
  Period                  M2 · period 1 (master's wiki)
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2} M2 program being finalized by the course instructors (the wiki indicates that the detailed M2 curriculum is still under development); course unit description confirmed by the wiki, SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who has already called a chat API / fine-tuned a small model and wants to know *why* token cost explodes, a RAG hallucinates, or DPO beats RLHF on a given budget. **Empirical first**: perplexity dropping with no usefulness; KV-cache OOM; leaderboard eval ≠ prod — then we name tokenizer, scaling, alignment.

Full LLM pipeline (tokenization → safety) as theory + labs. M2 pillar; most other modules plug into it. Official 24 h — this material deepens and flags additions.

### What you will be able to do

-   Explain the complete pipeline for building an LLM, from tokenization to post-training.
-   Implement alignment methods — SFT, RLHF, DPO, GRPO — and discuss their trade-offs.
-   Run an LLM in inference and master its costs and limits.
-   Build an in-depth RAG, beyond the basic tutorial.
-   Explore agents, multimodality and the perspectives they open.
-   Evaluate the performance and safety of an LLM with rigorous protocols.
-   Find your way in the literature and Shang's research work.

### Official objectives and syllabus

**Official description** (master's wiki): the SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet of this course unit is not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty); the description confirmed below is that of the wiki, which specifies the volume (24 h), credits (2 ECTS) and instructor. An immersion into LLMs, mixing essential theory and hands-on work to develop both practical skills and conceptual understanding — with a view to the LLM development and deployment professions: the syllabus starts with a brief panorama of historical NLP techniques, then addresses the transformer architecture (attention mechanism, tokenization) — the heart of modern LLMs —, the pre-training objectives (masked/denoising and causal language modeling, foundations of BERT, GPT and T5), the post-training techniques that refine a pre-trained model — instruction tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (PPO/DPO) and from verifiable rewards (GRPO) — and, finally, applications and future directions: RAG, agents, multimodality, alternative architectures. The following table maps these official themes to the sections of the material.

  Official syllabus theme (wiki)                                                              Course section covering it
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Panorama of historical NLP techniques                                                       ch. 0 “Background: from word2vec to transformers”

  Pre-training: masked/denoising and causal language modeling (BERT, GPT, T5)                 ch. 3 “Pre-training”
  Post-training: instruction tuning (SFT)                                                     ch. 4 “Post-training: SFT and alignment”

Beyond this official description, the material adds three deepenings: inference in practice (ch. 6), LLM evaluation and safety (ch. 9) and the reading of Shang's research (ch. 10).

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module (period 1), 24 h for 2 ECTS, M2 badge. Three M1 courses prepare it: [Introduction to Text Mining and NLP](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html) for text processing, [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) for the transformer architecture, and [Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) whose PPO sheds light on the RLHF and GRPO of the alignment chapter. Downstream, it is the gateway to [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html), [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html), [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) and [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Background: from word2vec to transformers** — the trajectory leading from word embeddings to the architecture at the center of the module.
-   **Tokenization** — how text becomes a sequence of tokens, and why this choice matters so much.
-   **The architecture in depth** — the transformer dissected: attention, blocks, variants and implementation details.
-   **Pre-training** — objectives, data and costs of the model's founding stage.
-   **Post-training: SFT and alignment** — going from the raw language model to the usable assistant.
-   **RLHF, DPO, GRPO** — reinforcement learning methods and their alternatives for aligning models.
-   **Running an LLM: inference** — serving a model: constraints, optimizations and costs.
-   **RAG in depth** — plugging models into external knowledge, seriously.
-   **Agents, multimodality and perspectives** — LLMs that act, see and listen.
-   **Evaluation and safety of LLMs** — measuring what models really do, and containing their risks.
-   **Research (Shang)** — the papers of Guokan Shang, read with the module's grid.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — hands-on sessions that follow each stage of the pipeline.
-   **References** — the papers and sources of each chapter.

### How to study this module

-   Do the labs alongside the chapters: the LLM pipeline is understood hands-on.
-   Keep the full pipeline in mind — tokenization, pre-training, alignment, inference — and place each new development in it.
-   Review the M1 reinforcement learning module before the RLHF chapter: PPO is assumed known there.
-   Read the key papers as you go: each chapter has one or two that sum it up.
-   For each method, ask what it costs in compute and data: that is often what decides in practice.
-   Test evaluation concepts on your own model outputs: measuring is harder than it looks.

::: note
[Extrapolons note]{.tag} LLM half of the master: M2 advanced / safety / MLOps / speech plug in; the graph half rejoins via GNN × LLM (Advanced GNN). LLM engineering or PhD: knowing *where* it breaks (tokens, cache, eval) matters as much as today's paper.
:::

## 0. Background: from word2vec to transformers {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1 modules)
:::

-   **Embeddings** (NLP ch. 3): word2vec/GloVe — a word = a *static* vector, derived skip-gram loss and negative sampling;
-   **Attention & transformers** (Deep Learning ch. 6): $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$, multi-head, residuals, LayerNorm; the "token graph" reading; BERT/GPT seen as applications (NLP ch. 7);
-   **Retrieval** (NLP ch. 2): TF-IDF and BM25 — the baselines of this module's retrieval (ch. 7); SBERT sentence embeddings (NLP ch. 7) for dense search;
-   **RL** (RL module): policies, policy gradients, PPO (ch. 4 of the RL module — the engine of alignment, ch. 5), bandits (ch. 6);
-   **Cross-entropy and perplexity** (ML ch. 3, NLP ch. 0): the pre-training loss is exactly maximum likelihood of the next token; $\mathrm{PPL}=\exp(\mathcal{L})$ in base e.
::::

**The trajectory**: n-grams → static embeddings → recurrent networks (LSTM) → attention (Bahdanau 2014) → transformer (Vaswani 2017) → BERT/GPT (2018-2019) → scaling (GPT-3, 2020) → alignment (InstructGPT 2022, RLHF) → general-purpose, multimodal, reasoning and agentic LLMs (2023-2026). This module covers every technical stage of this stack, from the tokenizer (ch. 1) to safety (ch. 9), proving results that M1 left as claims.

::: note
[Module methodology]{.tag} Each chapter alternates *proved theory* (thm/prop boxes with proofs) and *labs* (nanoGPT, toy DPO, RAG, agent). The "NLP ch. N" references point to the M1 module Introduction to Text Mining and NLP, of which this course is the direct continuation: tokenization (NLP ch. 1 → ch. 1), BM25 (NLP ch. 2 → ch. 7), sentence embeddings (NLP ch. 7 → ch. 7), transformers (NLP ch. 7 → ch. 2).
:::

## 1. Tokenization {#ch1}

Concrete scene: the same FR vs EN prompt on a Llama-style tokenizer. French typically costs 15–25% more tokens; your context budget melts, and a rare word splits into 6 subwords — the model "understands" less and bills more. This chapter fixes BPE / WordPiece / Unigram *before* architecture.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Mixing train/inference tokenizers; ignoring multilingual cost (latency + $); treating UNK as a detail. All three sabotage a prod RAG as much as a nanoGPT lab.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Byte-level BPE: the exact construction]{.tag} BPE (proved step by step in NLP ch. 1) starts here from the alphabet of 256 *bytes*: any Unicode string can be represented without an "unknown" symbol. Learning loop: $$\mathrm{merge}^{(k)} = \arg\max_{(a,b)}\; f(a,b),\qquad f(a,b)=\sum_{w}\mathrm{freq}(w)\,n_{(a,b)}(w),$$ where $n\_{(a,b)}(w)$ counts the occurrences of the adjacent pair $(a,b)$ in word $w$ (counting weighted by word frequency); the merge is applied everywhere and one starts again until $\|V\|$ (32k-128k). *Encoding* a new text replays the merges in the learned order (GPT-2/4, Llama); WordPiece (BERT) maximizes $\\frac{f(x,y)}{f(x)f(y)}$, Unigram (T5) learns a generative model by EM then segments with Viterbi (NLP ch. 1.2).
:::

::: note
[Vocabulary, compression, multilingual costs]{.tag} The compression rate (characters/token) depends on the vocabulary *and* the language: vocabularies trained on English compress English well (\~4 characters/token) but degrade other languages. Orders of magnitude measured in the lab: with GPT/Llama-type tokenizers, the same French text costs typically **15 to 25% more tokens** than in English; for poorly represented non-Latin scripts, the factor can reach **3× or more** (each rarely seen character decomposes into bytes). Direct consequences: API cost (billed per token), context length consumed, and inequality of quality. Llama 3 raised the vocabulary to 128k tokens — a large part of the gain serves non-English languages; GPT-4o (o200k) claims up to \~1.4× to \~4× fewer tokens depending on the language compared to the previous generation. Exercise 1 measures all this on your own texts.
:::

::: note
[Special tokens and security]{.tag} Special tokens (`<|endoftext|>`, `<|im_start|>`, template roles) delimit turns and documents. If the decoder accepts them in user input, an attacker can *inject* a fake dialogue turn or prematurely terminate a document (boundary confusion) — defense: systematically re-encode input and neutralize special tokens (`encode_ordinary`, the `allowed_special` flag of `tiktoken`), never raw string concatenation around the prompt. This class of attacks returns in ch. 9 (prompt injections).
:::

```python
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o")
okapi = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-3.5-turbo")   # cl100k vocabulary

fr = "Les graphes pour les LLMs : une révolution pour la recherche d'information."
de = "Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaftskapitän"
for s in (fr, de, "1234 + 5678 = ?"):
    print(len(okapi.encode(s)), "vs", len(enc.encode(s)), "->", s[:40])

# "safe" tokenization: special tokens are NOT decoded by default
b = enc.encode("fin <|endoftext|> suite", allowed_special=set())
print("ids :", b, "| decode round-trip ok :", enc.decode(b))
```

::: note
[Why it matters (M1 recall)]{.tag} Tokenization governs *cost* (length in tokens), *biases* (fuzzy arithmetic because "123 + 456" tokenizes poorly), *multilinguality* (the extra cost measured above) and real vulnerabilities (special tokens). Systematic diagnosis in the lab with `tiktoken` / `tokenizers`. For adapting an LLM to a low-resource language — vocabulary, template, data — ch. 10 presents Shang's work (Atlas-Chat, Nile-Chat).
:::

## 2. The architecture in depth {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — The decoder block]{.tag} An LLM stacks $N$ blocks: $$x \leftarrow x + \mathrm{MHA}(\mathrm{LN}(x)), \qquad x \leftarrow x + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(x)),$$ with **causal** attention (triangular mask: token $i$ sees only $j \\leq i$), grouped heads (*grouped-query attention* for inference), a gated MLP (SwiGLU, \~4× expansion), **RoPE** positional embeddings (rotations; relative generalization to long contexts), and a final LN.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Pre-norm vs post-norm: the gradient flow]{.tag} **Post-LN** (original transformer): $x\_{l+1}=\\mathrm{LN}(x_l+F(x_l))$ — each block renormalizes *the residual itself*; the gradient of $x_L$ to $x_0$ crosses $L$ LN Jacobians whose product decays/explodes exponentially with $L$: warmup mandatory, fragile depth. **Pre-LN** (GPT-2+, all modern LLMs): $x\_{l+1}=x_l+F(\\mathrm{LN}(x_l))$ — the residual path is *the identity*: $$\frac{\partial x_L}{\partial x_l} = I + \sum_{l'\,>\,l}\frac{\partial F_{l'}}{\partial x_l}$$ → a gradient that reaches every layer without multiplicative attenuation: stable training without fine warmup. Price: the norm $\|x_l\|$ grows with depth (additive contributions), hence the **final LN**. (Xiong et al., ICML 2020.)
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — RoPE derived (Su et al., 2021)]{.tag} Position is injected by rotation: the dimension-$d$ vector is viewed as $d/2$ 2D pairs; pair $i$ of the token at position $m$ undergoes $R(m\\theta_i)$ with $\\theta_i = 10000\^{-2i/d}$: $$R(\varphi)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{pmatrix}, \qquad q^{(i)}_m = R(m\theta_i)\,q^{(i)},\quad k^{(i)}_n = R(n\theta_i)\,k^{(i)}.$$

::: proof
**Relative property**: the dot product of a pair depends only on the *difference* of positions: $\\langle q\^{(i)}\_m,k\^{(i)}\_n\\rangle = q\^{(i)\\top} R(m\\theta_i)\^\\top R(n\\theta_i)\\, k\^{(i)} = q\^{(i)\\top} R\\big((n-m)\\theta_i\\big)\\,k\^{(i)}$, since 2D rotations commute and $R(a)\^\\top R(b)=R(b-a)$. Summing over pairs = an attention score depending on $(n-m)$ and the contents — a "soft" generalization of relative embeddings. Practical bonus: to extend the context, one *interpolates* the angles ($m\\to m/L$) instead of relearning. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — MQA/GQA: the memory arithmetic of the KV-cache]{.tag} The cache stores keys and values of all past tokens: $$\text{bytes/token} = 2\ (\text{K and V}) \times N_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{KV heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes/element}.$$ **Multi-Query Attention** (Shazeer, 2019): a single shared KV head; **Grouped-Query** (Ainslie et al., 2023): $n\_{\\text{KV}} < n\_{\\text{heads}}$ — e.g. Llama-3-8B: 32 heads, 8 KV heads, 32 layers, $d\_{\\text{head}}=128$, fp16 → $2\\times32\\times8\\times128\\times2 = 128\\,\\text{KiB/token}$; a 100k-token context ≈ **12.8 GB** of cache (versus \~51 GB with full attention — a 4× reduction, nearly identical quality). This is THE lever of long context (ch. 6).
:::

::: thm
[Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): routing and balancing]{.tag} Each MLP block is replaced by $E$ experts $\\{E_i\\}$; a router $g(x)=\\mathrm{softmax}(W_g x)$ activates only the top-$k$: $$y = \sum_{i\in \mathrm{top}\text{-}k} g_i(x)\,E_i(x), \qquad \#\text{active params} \ll \#\text{total params}.$$ Capacity decorrelated from inference cost (Switch Transformer: Fedus et al. 2021; DeepSeek-V3: 671B total, \~37B active). **Trap: routing collapse** — the winning experts attract everything. Auxiliary balancing loss (Switch): $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha\, E \sum_{i=1}^{E} f_i\,P_i,$$ $f_i$ = fraction of tokens routed to $i$, $P_i=\\frac{1}{T}\\sum_t g_i(x_t)$ = mean router probability; minimum reached at the uniform distribution ($f_i=P_i=1/E$) — zero penalty iff the router is balanced *and* confident. Modern variants: fine experts + *shared* experts, balancing without an auxiliary loss (dynamically adjusted bias, DeepSeek-V3).
:::

::: note
[Efficient attention: FlashAttention and IO complexity]{.tag} Exact attention costs $\\mathcal{O}(n\^2)$ compute but is *dominated in practice by input/output*: the naive implementation writes the $n\\times n$ matrix to HBM (large, slow memory). FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022): *exact* tiled computation that fits in SRAM, "online" softmax with an accumulator (running max $m$ and sum $\\ell$ updated per tile: $m\_{\\text{new}}=\\max(m,x)$, $\\ell\_{\\text{new}}=e\^{m-m\_{\\text{new}}}\\ell+e\^{x-m\_{\\text{new}}}$) — the $n\^2$ matrix is never materialized; HBM reads reduced from $\\Theta(n\^2)$ to $\\Theta(n\^2d\^2/M)$ ($M$ = SRAM size). The general lesson: *optimize memory access, not just FLOPs* (cf. Signal Processing module for the memory hierarchy).
:::

::: def
[Beyond: SSM/Mamba (state equation sketch)]{.tag} A state-space model discretizes a linear system $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t),\\ y=Cx$: $$x_k = \bar A x_{k-1} + \bar B u_k,\qquad y_k = C x_k,\qquad \bar A = e^{\Delta A},\ \bar B \approx \Delta B,$$ computable in $\\mathcal{O}(n)$ by a scan (no $n\^2$ matrix). The *selectivity* of Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023): $\\bar B, C, \\Delta$ depend on the input → content-dependent (selective forgetting), which yields attention quality at linear cost. SSD duality (Mamba-2, 2024): the same computation rewrites as $y_k=\\sum\_{s\\le k} C_k\^\\top\\big(\\prod\_{s<k'}\\bar A\\big)\\bar B_s\\,u_s$ — a "attention" with a causal kernel; hence the attention+SSM hybrid architectures. Continued in ch. 8.
:::

-   **Parameters: where are they?** embedding ($\|V\| \\times d$), attention ($4d\^2$/block), MLP ($8d\^2$/block, \~$12d\^2$/block with SwiGLU) — the rule $\\#\\text{params} \\approx 12 N d\^2$ and the training memory cost (parameters + Adam + activations + gradients: \~20 bytes/parameter in mixed precision; cf. ch. 3 for actual compute);
-   **LLGA bridge**: attention *is* message passing on a token graph (Graph ML module ch. 2, Advanced GNN); graph transformers inherit from it.

## 3. Pre-training {#ch3}

::: thm
[Pre-training objectives]{.tag}

-   **Causal modeling (CLM)** — GPT: $$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$$ — predict the next token; generative by construction;
-   **Masked modeling / denoising (MLM)** — BERT (NLP ch. 7): mask \~15% and predict (bidirectional); excellent for encoding (classification, retrieval), does not generate;
-   **Span corruption / text-to-text** — T5: mask spans and regenerate them; everything is formulated as sequence→sequence.
:::

### 3.1. The data pipeline: quality, filtering, deduplication

-   **Curation**: web → rule-based filtering (length, code/punctuation ratio, languages), then *model-based* filtering (quality classifiers trained on reference pages — e.g. distilled judges); controlled mixture (web, code, books, articles, mathematics, synthetic data generated then filtered);
-   **MinHash-LSH deduplication** (proved in NLP ch. 8.3): k-gram shingles → MinHash signatures (a min-hash collision has probability equal to the Jaccard similarity) → LSH bands/ranks with $\\mathbb{P}\_{\\text{detect}}(J)=1-(1-J\^r)\^b$ → remove near-duplicates down to a threshold. At scale: tens of TB of text, approximately linear clustering; measured effect: less memorization, better benchmark (*deduplicating is regularizing* — LLMs learn duplicates "twice");
-   **Mixtures and curriculum**: per-domain proportions (annealing: raise quality/lower web at the end of training); *easy→hard* ordering (by perplexity) improves compute efficiency — demonstrated at scale by Shang (ch. 10, "Beyond Random Sampling");
-   **Multilingual**: balancing per language (otherwise the tokenizer and the model drift toward English — cf. ch. 1 and 10).

### 3.2. Scaling laws: decomposition and the Chinchilla optimum

::: thm
[Combined law (Hoffmann et al. 2022, "Chinchilla")]{.tag} The loss of a model with $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens follows, over decades of scale: $$L(N,D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}},$$ $E$ = irreducible entropy of natural text; the other two terms = under-capacity and exhausted data (fitted on \~400 training runs; Kaplan et al. 2020 for the $L(N)$-only version). Reading: one must grow *N and D together*.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — The compute optimum $D\^\\star \\approx 20\\,N$, derived]{.tag} At fixed budget $C$, with $\\mathrm{FLOPs}(C) \\approx 6ND$ (2 per parameter × forward + backward, × D tokens): $$(N^\star, D^\star) = \arg\min_{N,D}\; L(N,D)\quad \text{s.t.}\quad 6ND = C.$$

::: proof
Lagrangian $\\mathcal{J}=E+AN\^{-\\alpha}+BD\^{-\\beta}-\\lambda(6ND-C)$: $$\frac{\partial\mathcal{J}}{\partial N}= -\alpha A N^{-\alpha-1}-6\lambda D=0, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal{J}}{\partial D}= -\beta B D^{-\beta-1}-6\lambda N=0.$$ Dividing side by side, $\\lambda$ cancels: $$\frac{\alpha A\,N^{-\alpha-1}}{\beta B\,D^{-\beta-1}} = \frac{D}{N} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\,D^{\beta} = N^{\alpha} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{N^{\alpha}}{D^{\beta}} = \frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}.$$ With Chinchilla's fitted constants ($\\alpha\\approx0.34$, $\\beta\\approx0.28$, $A\\approx406$, $B\\approx411$): the right-hand side equals $\\approx 1.2$, and the condition together with $6ND=C$ gives $N\^\\star\\propto C\^{0.46}$, $D\^\\star\\propto C\^{0.54}$ — *both grow like $\\sqrt{C}$*, and numerically $D\^\\star/N\^\\star\\approx 20$ tokens per parameter. GPT-3 (300B tokens for 175B params, ratio 1.7) was therefore "undertrained" at its budget. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Compute and real costs (Llama 3, 2024)]{.tag} Orders of magnitude from the Llama 3 technical report (H100 training): 8B / 15T tokens ≈ 1.5M GPU-hours; 70B ≈ 7M; 405B / 15.6T tokens ≈ 30.8M GPU-hours (≈ 3.5 years of a single H100 × 10⁴). At \~2-3 $/GPU-hour, the 405B costs \~80-90M$ of compute — why one "continues" from checkpoints rather than retraining (ch. 6: distillation, LoRA); and why the post-Chinchilla ratio went up: since inference costs daily, one deliberately *overtrains* small models (Llama-3-8B: 15T tokens ≈ 1900 tokens per parameter, \~100× Chinchilla) — the optimum depends on what is being optimized: the *training cost* (Chinchilla) or the *total cost* including inference.
:::

::: ex
[Lab: training a mini-GPT]{.tag} On a Shakespeare-type corpus (\~1 MB), train a \~10M-parameter transformer (nanoGPT): 30 minutes of GPU suffice to generate credible text. Observe: the loss curve, the effect of context, the sampling temperature (ch. 6). Extend: do exercise 4 (check the law $L(N,D)$ by regression on the published points).
:::

## 4. Post-training: SFT and alignment {#ch4}

::: def
[Step 1 — Supervised Fine-Tuning (instruction tuning)]{.tag} Fine-tune the base model on quality (instruction, response) pairs — a few tens/hundreds of thousands of examples suffice to turn an autocomplete into an assistant. Engineering details: loss mask (the loss is computed only on the response), chat templates, data "distilled" from a large model.
:::

::: def
[Templates and loss mask — the detail that matters]{.tag} The template serializes the turns: `<|system|>…<|user|>…<|assistant|>`. The loss masks the *prompt* tokens (system/user roles) and keeps only the *completion* — otherwise the model learns to *imitate the user* and prompt logging becomes noise: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = -\sum_{t\,\in\,\text{completion}} \log p_\theta(y_t\mid y_{<t}, x).$$
:::

```python
# SFT with loss masking (HF TRL pseudo-code)
from trl import SFTTrainer

def format(example):                    # chat template + masked labels
    prompt  = f"<|user|>\n{example['question']}\n<|assistant|>\n"
    completion = example["answer"]
    return {"prompt": prompt, "completion": completion}
# - the loss is computed ONLY on the completion tokens (TRL SFTTrainer
#   does the masking automatically; in raw PyTorch: labels = -100 on the prompt)

trainer = SFTTrainer(model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B",
                     train_dataset=dataset.map(format), ...)
trainer.train()

# pitfalls seen in the lab: template != inference template -> performance drop;
# padding token confused with eos; overly long answers -> silent truncation
```

::: def
[Step 2 — Why alignment beyond SFT?]{.tag} SFT imitates demonstrations; it does not directly optimize "the best response" and does not learn to avoid harmful responses. The central idea of InstructGPT/ChatGPT: **learn a human reward**, then optimize the policy against that reward (RL) — this is where the M1 RL module becomes the M2's central tool.
:::

::: note
[Rejection sampling (best-of-n)]{.tag} An intermediate and indestructible step: generate $n$ responses, keep those that pass a filter (reward model, tests, heuristics), re-fine-tune on them — the Llama 2 recipe between RLHF rounds (Touvron et al., 2023). This is exactly "exploit the best of $n$", without policy gradients; the link with bandits (RL module ch. 6) is direct: each draw informs the policy for the next round.
:::

## 5. RLHF, DPO, GRPO {#ch5}

::: thm
[RLHF — the classic pipeline (Ouyang et al., 2022)]{.tag}

1.  **Reward model**: train $r\_\\phi(x, y)$ on *human preferences* (response pairs); Bradley-Terry loss: $$\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y^+) - r_\phi(x, y^-)\big).$$
2.  **Policy optimization** with PPO (RL module, ch. 4): $$\max_\theta\ \mathbb{E}\big[r_\phi(x, y)\big] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}\big)$$ — the KL term prevents *reward hacking* and out-of-distribution drift.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Bradley-Terry, derived]{.tag} If humans compare pairs $(y\^+,y\^-)$ with a probability of preferring $y\^+$ increasing in the "strength" difference, the axiomatics (transitive binary choice, invariance) imposes a logistic model on the *difference* of latent scores: $$\mathbb{P}(y^+ \succ y^- \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x,y^+)-r(x,y^-)\big),$$ and the log-likelihood of the observed preferences gives the loss above — only the *difference* of rewards is identifiable (adding a function of $x$ changes nothing); hence the need for the KL penalty to pin down the zero.

::: proof
Derivative in $r\^+$: $-\\big(1-\\sigma(r\^+-r\^-)\\big)$ — the penalty is maximal when the pair is misclassified, zero when the margin is amply positive; it is a logistic regression on reward differences. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[PPO for LLMs — the concrete protocol]{.tag} Four models in memory: policy $\\pi\_\\theta$, reference $\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}}$ (frozen, for the KL), reward $r\_\\phi$ (frozen), critic (value head). Sensitive hyperparameters: $\\beta\\in[0.01,\\,0.2]$; *low* learning rate (≈ 10× smaller than in SFT); PPO clip $\\epsilon\\sim0.2$; prompt batch > completion batch. Classic symptoms: KL explodes (β too small); degenerate responses (hacked reward); drifting length (RM verbosity bias). This is chapter 4 of the RL module applied word for word — the prerequisite reading.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): complete derivation]{.tag} The loss $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\Big(\beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y^+ \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y^+\mid x)} - \beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y^- \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y^-\mid x)}\Big)$$ optimizes *the policy directly* on preferences — without a reward model or rollouts.

::: proof
**Step 1 (closed-form solution of the KL-penalized problem).** For fixed $x$, maximizing $\\mathbb{E}\_{y\\sim\\pi}[r(y)] - \\beta\\,\\mathrm{KL}(\\pi\|\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}})$ rewrites as $$\max_\pi \int \pi(y)\Big[r(y) - \beta\log\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y)}\Big]dy = -\beta\int \pi\log\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y)e^{r(y)/\beta}}\,dy,$$ which is $-\\beta\\,\\mathrm{KL}\\big(\\pi\\,\\big\|\\,\\tfrac{1}{Z}\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}}e\^{r/\\beta}\\big)+\\beta\\log Z$; the KL is minimal at zero, so $\\;\\pi\^\\star(y\\mid x) = \\frac{1}{Z(x)}\\,\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}}(y\\mid x)\\,e\^{r(x,y)/\\beta}$. **Step 2 (implicit reward).** Inverting: $r(x,y) = \\beta\\log\\frac{\\pi\^\\star(y\|x)}{\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}}(y\|x)} + \\beta\\log Z(x)$. **Step 3 (injection into Bradley-Terry).** In $\\sigma(r\^+-r\^-)$, the term $Z(x)$ — the same for $y\^+$ and $y\^-$ — *cancels*: only the difference of log-ratios matters; maximizing the likelihood of the preferences gives $\\mathcal{L}\_{\\mathrm{DPO}}$ above (with $\\theta$ in place of $\\pi\^\\star$). **Gradient**: $-\\beta\\,\\sigma(-\\hat r)\\,\\nabla\_\\theta\\big[\\log\\pi(y\^+\|x)-\\log\\pi(y\^-\|x)\\big]$ with implicit reward $\\hat r = \\beta\\log\\frac{\\pi\_\\theta(y\^+)}{\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}}(y\^+)} -\\beta\\log\\frac{\\pi\_\\theta(y\^-)}{\\pi\_{\\mathrm{SFT}}(y\^-)}$: the log-ratio margin of the preferred responses is increased, all the more strongly as the pair is misclassified. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — GRPO (Shao et al., DeepSeekMath 2024): derivation]{.tag} Generate a *group* of $G$ responses $\\{y_i\\}$ per prompt; rewards $\\{r_i\\}$; advantages *within the group*: $$A_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_{1..G})}{\mathrm{std}(r_{1..G})},\qquad \nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{G}\sum_i \frac{1}{\|y_i\|}\sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x)\,A_i\Big] - \beta\,\nabla_\theta \widehat{\mathrm{KL}},$$ with $\\widehat{\\mathrm{KL}}$ an unbiased, low-variance estimator $\\;\\mathbb{E}\\big[\\frac{\\pi\_{\\mathrm{ref}}}{\\pi\_\\theta}-\\log\\frac{\\pi\_{\\mathrm{ref}}}{\\pi\_\\theta}-1\\big]$.

::: proof
**Variance.** REINFORCE: $\\nabla\\mathbb{E}[r]=\\mathbb{E}[r\\,\\nabla\\log\\pi]$ is unbiased for any *baseline* independent of the action: $\\mathbb{E}[b\\,\\nabla\\log\\pi]=b\\,\\nabla\\!\\int\\pi=0$; subtracting $b=\\mathrm{mean}(r)$ divides the variance (better than $b=0$ or a learned baseline); normalizing by the standard deviation makes the gradient scale invariant across prompts (easy ones: small spreads → amplified; hard ones: damped). **No more critic.** Unlike PPO, the baseline comes from *the group itself* — the value network (and its memory/training) disappears; it is the Monte-Carlo estimation of $A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s)$ by multiple sampling. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[RLVR and reasoning (2024-2026)]{.tag} When quality is **verifiable** (a passing unit test, an exact mathematical answer), the reward no longer needs to be learned: *RL with Verifiable Rewards*. GRPO is the engine of DeepSeek-R1: by optimizing verifiable correctness, *long chains of thought* emerge (self-verification, backtracking, "aha" moments) — the "o1" style. **Self-consistency** at inference (Wang et al., 2023): sample $n$ reasonings, answer by *majority vote* — accuracy climbing at $\\Theta(\\sqrt n)$-ish as long as errors are weakly correlated. Costs: 10× more tokens; recent works regularize length (ch. 10: "Shorter but not Worse"). Exploration (bandits, RL module ch. 6) becomes central: the GRPO group *is* structured exploration.
:::

::: note
[Overview]{.tag} SFT (imitate) → RLHF (optimize preferences) → DPO (preferences without RL) → RLVR/GRPO (optimize verifiable truth). A "modern" LLM chains: base → SFT → rejection sampling → DPO/GRPO; this is exactly the plan of the official course ("post-training methods"). In the lab: toy DPO (exercise 7) then GRPO (exercise 8).
:::

## 6. Running an LLM: inference {#ch6}

### 6.1. Decoding: formulas and effects

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — From greedy to nucleus]{.tag} At each step, logits $z$ over $\|V\|$;

-   **Temperature**: $p_i = \\dfrac{\\exp(z_i/T)}{\\sum_j \\exp(z_j/T)}$ — $T\\to0$: argmax (greedy); large $T$: uniformization;
-   **Top-k**: truncate to the $k$ best logits then renormalize;
-   **Top-p (nucleus)**: smallest set of tokens with cumulative probability $\\ge p$ (*adaptive* size: wide on an uncertain step, narrow on a deterministic step);
-   **Repetition penalty**: divide the logit of already emitted tokens (factor 1.1-1.3); **min-p**: threshold relative to the best token.
:::

  Setting                        Effect on quality                     Effect on diversity   Use
  ------------------------------ ------------------------------------- --------------------- -------------------------------
  T = 0 (greedy)                 deterministic, possible repetitions   none                  extraction, code, factual RAG
  Moderate T (0.7) + top-p 0.9   fluent, controlled                    moderate              general dialogue
  High T (1.0+), top-p 0.95      more hallucinations                   strong                brainstorming, synthetic data

### 6.2. KV-cache: the memory arithmetic

::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Cache memory = $\\mathcal{O}(n\\cdot d)$, quantified]{.tag} In autoregression, each new token must attend to the keys/values of the whole past — they are cached (prop. 2.4): bytes/token $= 2\\,N\_{\\text{layers}}\\,n\_{\\text{KV}}\\,d\_{\\text{head}}\\times$ precision. **Llama-3-8B** (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim, fp16) → 128 KiB/token: 8k context ≈ 1 GB, 100k ≈ 12.8 GB, 1M ≈ 128 GB (weights excluded!). Three ways out: GQA (÷4 here), int8 cache quantization (÷2), and eviction/recomputation (sliding window). Engineering rule: *context length is first a memory bandwidth problem*, not a FLOPs problem — hence the next chapter.
:::

### 6.3. Speculative decoding: the correction proved

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023)]{.tag} A small model $q$ proposes $\\gamma$ tokens; the large model $p$ computes the $\\gamma$ distributions *in a single forward*; each proposal $y$ is accepted with probability $\\min(1, p(y)/q(y))$; at the first rejection, one resamples from the normalized residual $\\mathrm{norm}\\big(\\max(0,\\,p-q)\\big)$. Then the marginal distribution of each produced token is *exactly* $p$ — quality unchanged, latency divided by \~2-3 when $q\\approx p$.

::: proof
For one token: acceptance contribution $q(y)\\min(1,p(y)/q(y)) = \\min(q(y),p(y))$; rejection contribution: the total rejected mass equals $\\sum_x q(x)\\big(1-\\min(1,p(x)/q(x))\\big) = \\sum_x \\max(0,q(x)-p(x)) = R$, and the resampled residual adds $R\\cdot\\frac{\\max(0,p(y)-q(y))}{R} = \\max(0,p(y)-q(y))$. Total: $\\min(q,p)+\\max(0,p-q)=p$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 6.4. Quantization: principles and errors

-   **Post-training int8**: nearly lossless (batch calibration, per-channel scales); **int4**: the standard compromise;
-   **GPTQ** (Frantar et al., 2022): layer by layer, minimize $\|Wx-\\hat W x\|\_2\^2$ on a calibration set — column-by-column quantization *with error compensation* on the remaining columns (via the inverse of the Hessian $\\mathbf{H}=2\\mathbf{X}\\mathbf{X}\^\\top$);
-   **AWQ** (Lin et al., 2023): protect the "salient" channels (high activations) with per-channel scaling *before* quantization — the error is shifted toward weakly active channels;
-   **Typical errors**: int8 ≈ +0.0-0.1 PPL; well-calibrated int4 ≈ +0.1-0.5 PPL (often imperceptible); below 4 bits, degradation accelerates (2-3-bit quantization = research); in production, always re-validate on *your* benchmarks, not PPL alone.

### 6.5. Serving: continuous batching, PagedAttention, costs

-   **Continuous batching** (vLLM, Orca): schedule at the *decoding step* — finished sequences leave, new ones enter the same batch; throughput multiplied by \~10-20× vs static batching;
-   **PagedAttention** (Kwon et al., 2023): the KV-cache split into pages (like virtual memory) — no more fragmentation; sharing of common prefixes (system prompt); \~2-4× memory gain → larger batches;
-   **Costs**: two regimes — API (on the order of $/M tokens, steadily decreasing) vs on-prem (amortized GPU-hour: an H100 at \~3$/h serving \~2-5k tokens/s on an int4-quantized 8B → a few $/M tokens under heavy load); the real cost of an agent = repeated input tokens × history length (ch. 8); the "ML Ops" angle is deepened in the dedicated M2 module.

```python
# KV-cache arithmetic (cf. prop. 6.2): Llama-3-8B
L, kv_heads, d_head, bytes = 32, 8, 128, 2
per_tok = 2 * L * kv_heads * d_head * bytes      # bytes / token
for ctx in (8_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
    print(f"context {ctx//1000:4d}k -> {per_tok*ctx/2**30:6.1f} GiB of KV-cache")

# speculative decoding in one line (HF): small = proposes, large = verifies
from transformers import SpeculativeDecodingSpec  # (illustrative; cf. vLLM lab)
# result: outputs IDENTICAL in distribution to the large model alone (thm 6.3)
```

## 7. RAG in depth {#ch7}

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)]{.tag} $$p(y \mid q) \approx p_\theta\big(y \mid q, \mathrm{top}_k\, \mathrm{sim}(e_q, e_d)\big)$$ index documents by embeddings, retrieve those closest to the prompt, inject them into the context. Reduces hallucinations, updates knowledge, handles proprietary data *without retraining*.
:::

### 7.1. Chunking

-   **Fixed with overlap**: 256-1024 tokens, stride 10-20%; *structural* splitting (sections, paragraphs) > blind splitting (cut sentences destroy retrieval);
-   **Semantic chunking**: cut where the embedding similarity between successive windows drops (topic change);
-   **Multi-granularity**: index by passages, but return the parent section to the LLM (small-to-big); for structured documents, keep titles/metadata in the chunk (pre-retrieval filters).

### 7.2. Retrieval: BM25, dense, hybrid — with numbers

  Retriever           Principle                             BEIR (NDCG@10, \~18 tasks)   Strengths / weaknesses
  ------------------- ------------------------------------- ---------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------
  BM25                probabilistic weighting (NLP ch. 2)   ≈ 0.44 on average            zero training, exact (lexical matches); misses reformulations
  Dense (E5/BGE, …)   SBERT embeddings + ANN (FAISS/HNSW)   ≈ 0.50-0.52 for the best     captures paraphrase; errors on jargon/exact refs, must be indexed
  Hybrid + reranker   fusion (RRF) then cross-encoder       ≈ 0.53-0.55                  practical state of the art; reranking cost O(top-100)

::: note
[Cross-encoder rerankers]{.tag} The bi-encoder scores $s(q,d)=\cos(e_q,e_d)$ *separately* (indexable); the cross-encoder scores $s(q,d)=f_\theta([q\,;d])$ *jointly* — it sees the exact term interaction (mini-attention) but must run on every candidate; hence the cascade architecture: dense/BM25 (top-100) → cross-encoder (top-5). Typical gain: +3 to +5 points of NDCG@10. The "lost in the middle" effect (Liu et al., 2023): even with the right passages, the LLM exploits better those at the beginning/end of the context → reorder the best ones *at the extremes*.
:::

### 7.3. RAG evaluation

::: def
[RAGAS-type metrics (Es et al., 2023)]{.tag}

-   **Faithfulness**: decompose the answer into atomic claims (by an LLM judge); faithfulness = fraction *supported by the retrieved context*;
-   **Answer relevance**: the LLM generates candidate questions from the answer — average similarity with the true question;
-   **Context precision / recall**: are the useful chunks there and well ranked? / does the corpus contain what was missing?

Lab protocol: QA set with reference context (*golden context*), compare faithfulness with/without reranking, measure the cost (tokens, latency) of each stage.
:::

### 7.4. GraphRAG and variants

-   **HyDE** (Gao et al., 2022): generate a *hypothetical answer* to the question and search *with its embedding* — the imaginary answer is closer to the documents than the question;
-   **GraphRAG**: retrieval traverses a *knowledge graph* (entity-relation extraction by NER/RE — NLP ch. 6; communities-summaries; multi-hop queries); detailed in the Graph ML module ch. 8 — the LLGA heart; Buscaldi's work (AI-KG/CS-KG, NLP ch. 9) builds exactly such graphs from scientific corpora;
-   **Structured queries**: text → graph query (linearization, ch. 10.3) or SQL (text-to-SQL): the LLM writes the query, the database answers — maximal auditability.

```python
# minimal RAG (pseudocode with sentence-transformers + FAISS)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import faiss, numpy as np

enc = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
idx = faiss.IndexFlatIP(384); idx.add(enc.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True))

def answer(question, k=4):
    D, I = idx.search(enc.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True), k)
    context = "\n".join(chunks[i] for i in I[0])
    prompt = f"Réponds selon le contexte suivant :\n{context}\n\nQuestion : {question}"
    return llm.chat(prompt)   # + citations = retrieved sources

# lab extension: cross-encoder reranking on the top-20, then
# RAGAS evaluation (faithfulness / answer relevance) on 30 questions.
```

## 8. Agents, multimodality and perspectives {#ch8}

### 8.1. The ReAct loop, with a real trace

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — LLM agent (ReAct, Yao et al., 2022)]{.tag} Perception-action loop (RL module ch. 7): **Thought** (reason) → **Action** (call a tool) → **Observation** (read the result) → iterate, until *Final Answer*. The LLM decides *when* and *how* to act; the tools bound its capabilities (exact computation, search, code).
:::

```python
Question : quel module du M1 couvre les HMM ?

Thought: je dois chercher dans le programme du master.
Action: search["programme M1 NLP HMM"]
Observation: ... CSC_52082_EP "Introduction to Text Mining and NLP",
             ch. 6 "Sequences: NER, HMM, CRF" ...
Thought: la réponse est dans la liste des chapitres.
Action: finish["Le module NLP (CSC_52082_EP), chapitre 6"]

# modern function calling: JSON typed by the chat engine
tools = [{"type": "function", "name": "search",
          "parameters": {"query": "str", "k": "int"}}]
# the model emits {"name": "search", "arguments": {"query": "...", "k": 5}}
# -> the runtime executes, reinjects the result, and the loop continues
```

::: note
[Planning and multi-agents]{.tag}

-   **Tree-of-Thoughts** (Yao et al., 2023): search a *tree* of reasoning steps, evaluate the nodes with the LLM, backtrack — beyond the linear chain (CoT);
-   **Multi-agents**: orchestrate a **DAG** of specialized agents (planner → retriever/coder → verifier → synthesis), LangGraph-type frameworks; each agent = an LLM with its own prompt/tools/memory; patterns: supervisor, debate, generator-critic. RL link ch. 7: policy decomposition; Graph ML link: *orchestration is an executed graph*;
-   **Memory**: scratchpad (the current context), *vector* memory (RAG over past exchanges), *episodic* memory (structured session summaries), external working memory (files) — it is the ch. 7 RAG reused on oneself.
:::

::: note
[Evaluating (and billing) an agent]{.tag} Benchmarks: GAIA (generalist assistant), SWE-bench (real GitHub tickets), WebArena/tau-bench (tools and dialogues). Metrics: end-to-end success rate, *token cost per task* (a multi-turn agent easily consumes 10⁵-10⁶ tokens — hence the importance of ch. 6: a small model for routine steps, a large one for decisions), safety (rate of injections suffered — ch. 9). Agent evaluation is an open research topic — and a major career path of the master.
:::

### 8.2. Multimodality: how an image enters a context

-   **Vision**: a ViT encoder cuts the image into 16×16 patches → *one token per patch* (Deep Learning module ch. 5 for ViT); a **projector** (MLP or Q-Former) aligns these tokens onto the LLM's embedding space → the image becomes "text" inside the context (LLaVA scheme); the encoder is often pre-trained contrastively image-text — the common latent space recalls CLIP (Multimodal GenAI module ch. 5);
-   **Audio**: mel spectrograms → encoder (Whisper-style) → tokens; the "transcription + style" output feeds the LLM (voice assistant = encoder → LLM → synthesis pipeline);
-   **Video**: sampled images (1-4/s) + temporal pooling — very high token cost: the sampling step choice *is* a compression choice;
-   **Documents**: pages = images + interleaved OCR text (the number 1 enterprise use case — contracts, reports).

### 8.3. Perspectives

-   **Alternative architectures**: attention+SSM hybrids (ch. 2), xLSTM, latent transformers (deraising diffusion LMs — cf. ch. 10); the transformer does not have a monopoly;
-   **Small Language Models & distillation**: the quality/cost/latency trade-off governs enterprise deployment (ch. 6);
-   **Open research**: reasoning (ch. 5), long-term memory, LLMs *on graphs* (linearization vs structured embeddings — ch. 10.3 and the Graph ML/Advanced GNN modules), evaluation (ch. 9).

::: ex
[Final lab]{.tag} Build a documentation-assistant: technical corpus → RAG pipeline (chunks, embeddings, reranking); measure faithfulness (verifiable citations) for vector RAG versus a *GraphRAG* version; cost report (tokens, latency). Extension: an agentic version (ch. 8) that chooses between vector retrieval and a graph query depending on the question type.
:::

## 9. Evaluation and safety of LLMs {#ch9}

### 9.1. Benchmarks: construction and contamination

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — MMLU-type benchmark (Hendrycks et al., 2020)]{.tag} Multiple-choice questions (57 subjects for MMLU; variants: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HELM for multi-faceted evaluation). Two scoring modes: *log-likelihood* of the options (deterministic, but biased by answer length/frequency) vs *generation* then extraction (realistic, but prompt- and parsing-dependent). Rule: always specify the protocol — rankings change with the mode.
:::

::: note
[Contamination: the measurement that skews everything]{.tag} If the benchmark is in the pre-training data (the web!), the score measures *memorization*, not competence. Detection: n-gram overlap (8-13 grams) between questions/training data, canary strings (hidden markers), cloze recall tests. Remedies: private/rotating evaluations, dynamic question generation, temporal re-splits (post-cutoff questions). Recent work on this: memorization in fine-tuning and multilingual hallucinations — ch. 10 of the M1 NLP module (Buscaldi's work: MUCH, memorization prediction).
:::

### 9.2. LLM-as-judge: convenient, but biased

-   **Positional bias**: the judge prefers the first (or second) answer depending on order — mitigation: evaluate in both orders and average;
-   **Verbosity / style bias**: long, well-formatted answers are overrated — mitigation: rubrics (explicit criteria), constrained format;
-   **Self-preference**: a judge favors answers from its own model family — mitigation: judge ensembles, judges trained for calibration (references: MT-Bench, G-Eval);
-   **Calibration**: a judge score is not a probability — verify on a set where ground truth exists (fraction of judgments matching humans); cheap *distilled* metrics (FrugalScore, ch. 10) were born exactly from this need.

### 9.3. Hallucinations

::: def
[Taxonomy 9.2]{.tag} **Intrinsic**: the answer contradicts the source/context (RAG: wrong citation); **extrinsic**: unverifiable (invented) claims; **prompt fidelity**: silent disobedience to instructions. Causes: sampling (temperature), knowledge cutoff, the "always answer" training bias (no learned abstention), sycophancy (telling the user yes). Mitigations: RAG + verifiable citations (ch. 7), self-consistency (ch. 5), low temperature for factual tasks, abstention training, post-hoc verification by decomposition into claims (the heart of RAGAS "faithfulness").
:::

### 9.4. Attacks: jailbreaks and prompt injections

-   **Direct jailbreaks**: role-play ("DAN"), hypothetical framing, encoding (base64, unicode), multi-turn crescendo — circumventing safety instructions;
-   **Indirect injections**: the *retrieved content* (web page, PDF, tool result) contains malicious instructions — the number 1 attack on RAG/agent systems (ch. 7-8);
-   **Defense in depth**: input/output classifiers (Llama Guard type), *spotlighting* (delimiting and marking untrusted content), least privilege on tools (the retriever does not write to the database!), prompt/data separation (ch. 1 — special tokens: the same hygiene), human in the loop for irreversible actions. No defense is complete — one *reduces* the attack surface.

### 9.5. Watermarking

:::: thm
[Theorem 9.3 — Statistical watermark (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023)]{.tag} Before each token, hash the prefix → a pseudo-random seed that partitions the vocabulary into "green"/"red" (fraction $\gamma$, e.g. 1/2); generation penalizes reds. On a text of $T$ tokens containing $s_G$ green ones: $$z = \frac{s_G - \gamma T}{\sqrt{T\,\gamma(1-\gamma)}} \;\xrightarrow{T\ \text{large}}\; \mathcal{N}(0,1)\ \text{under H}_0,$$ reject "human text" if $z$ exceeds the threshold (p-value) — under H1 (marked), $z$ grows like $\sqrt T$ times the introduced bias.

::: proof
Under H₀ (unmarked text), each token is green with probability $\gamma$ independently → $s_G\sim\mathrm{Bin}(T,\gamma)$, the standardized variable tends to the normal (CLT), hence the z-score; the partition depends on the *prefix*: impossible to remove without the seed. Limitations (follow-up paper, Kirchenbauer et al. 2023): paraphrasing, truncation, and false positives on short texts — the test is statistical, not deterministic. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

## 10. Research (Shang) {#ch10}

Guokan Shang (lead research scientist, MBZUAI; PhD at the LIX laboratory, École Polytechnique, 2021, under the supervision of M. Vazirgiannis — the LLGA loop) works on the evaluation of generative models, efficient pre-training, multilingual LLMs and dialogue summarization. Three axes presented in detail, then the rest of the filmography, each positioned relative to the chapters.

::: thm
[Axis 1 — Frugal evaluation: FrugalScore (ACL 2022)]{.tag} *Kamal Eddine, Shang, Tixier & Vazirgiannis, FrugalScore: Learning Cheaper, Lighter and Faster Evaluation Metrics for Automatic Text Generation* — [arXiv:2110.08559](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08559). **Problem**: neural generation metrics (BERTScore, MoverScore…) cost one large-model forward *per pair* — prohibitive in a learning or LLM-judge evaluation loop. **Method**: *distill* the reference metric (the scores, not the texts!) into a tiny student (T5-small), with an input representation compatible with the mother metric. **Result**: correlation nearly preserved for a cost reduced by a factor of up to \~700× (plus pre-trained V2 variants). **Position:** the "evaluation at an industrializable price" link of ch. 9 — evaluate often, at low cost, before evaluating well (heavy judges) on a subsample.
:::

::: thm
[Axis 2 — Curriculum in pre-training: Beyond Random Sampling (EACL 2026)]{.tag} *Zhang, Mohamed, Abdine, Shang & Vazirgiannis, Beyond Random Sampling: Efficient Language Model Pretraining via Curriculum Learning* — [arXiv:2506.11300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11300). **Question**: does the order of pre-training data (ch. 3) matter, at constant compute? **Method**: first systematic large-scale study (several hundred models, from 50M to 1M parameters): curriculum by difficulty (perplexity, quality) easy→hard vs random mixtures. **Result**: the curriculum improves the loss at fixed budget (better compute efficiency), with granularity choices that matter. **Position:** the "curriculum & annealing" content of ch. 3 builds on this paper — an example of an engineering question (in what order to feed the model?) turned into measurable science.
:::

::: thm
[Axis 3 — LLMs for low-resource languages: Atlas-Chat & Nile-Chat (2024-2025)]{.tag} *Shang et al., Atlas-Chat: Adapting Large Language Models for Low-Resource Moroccan Arabic Dialect* — [arXiv:2409.17912](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17912) (1B/2B/3B models on 223B tokens of dialect; templates, SFT + DPO); *Nile-Chat: Egyptian Language Models for Arabic and Latin Scripts* — [arXiv:2507.04569](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04569) (handling *arabizi* — Arabic in Latin script — at the tokenizer and pre-training level). **Position:** ch. 1 (multilingual costs, vocabulary) and ch. 4 (SFT/DPO) applied to a real problem: adapting the LLM ecosystem to languages/scripts that dominant vocabularies penalize — the logical continuation of the extra-cost measurements done in the lab.
:::

::: note
[The rest of the filmography (with positioning)]{.tag}

-   **Meeting summarization** (the PhD thread): [unsupervised abstractive summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.05271) by multi-sentence compression + budgeted submodular maximization (ACL 2018 — the "graphical text mining" of M1 NLP ch. 8); [self-attentive abstractive communities](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09491) (AACL 2020); [speaker-change-aware CRF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.02913) for dialogue acts (COLING 2020 — the CRFs of M1 NLP ch. 6); TACL 2023 survey ([arXiv:2208.04163](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04163)); French corpora [FREDSum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04843) (political debates) and [Claire](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16840) (spontaneous French dialogue); back to extraction: [discourse and extractive summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11055) (2024);
-   **LLM faithfulness and diversity**: "LLM as a Broken Telephone" (ACL 2025, [arXiv:2502.20258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.20258)) — iterative generation distorts information (ch. 9); benchmark of [linguistic diversity of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10271) (TACL 2025); Markov generation chains (2026, [arXiv:2603.11228](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11228));
-   **Frugal RLVR**: "Shorter but not Worse" (2025, [arXiv:2511.01937](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01937)) — regularizing the length of math RLVR reasonings (ch. 5);
-   **Graphs & LLMs**: [graph linearization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19494) methods for reasoning with an LLM (ch. 7 — GraphRAG; bridge toward the Graph ML/Advanced GNN modules).
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **Multilingual tokenization.** Compare BPE vs Unigram vs SentencePiece on a multilingual corpus: compression (characters/token), coverage of numbers; measure the French "extra cost" over English for the same text.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): aligned professional translations (fr/en/de) → tokens/word; typically fr ≈ 1.15-1.25× en; German with compounds even more — until frequent compounds become tokens; check that o200k (GPT-4o) narrows the gap vs cl100k. Conclude on the real cost (context, API price) of the same application depending on the language. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **RoPE.** Prove the relative property of thm 2.3 ($R(a)^\top R(b) = R(b-a)$), then check numerically that the attention score is invariant under a common translation of positions; implement context interpolation $m\to m/L$ and measure perplexity beyond the training length.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: 2D rotations = complex numbers — commutativity and $e^{-ia}e^{ib}=e^{i(b-a)}$; translation invariance follows from the theorem; in practice naive extrapolation degrades PPL, interpolation largely preserves it (this is the basis of extended contexts 32k→128k without full retraining). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **KV-cache arithmetic.** For Llama-3-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim) and a 128k-token context: compute the cache memory in fp16, then in int8, then with MQA; what maximum batch fits on an 80 GB GPU (int4 weights ≈ 5 GB)?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: 128 KiB/token (prop. 2.4) → 128k tokens = 16 GiB; int8 → 8 GiB; MQA (1 KV head) → 2 GiB; available budget ≈ 80−5 = 75 GiB → batch of \~4 (fp16) to \~37 (MQA int8): GQA/MQA and cache quantization *determine* the served throughput. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **Scaling.** From published data (LLaMA 1/2/3, Chinchilla), verify the law $\mathcal{L} \approx A N^{-\alpha} + B D^{-\beta} + E$ by regression; situate each model relative to the compute optimum (thm 3.1).
5.  **MoE.** Derive the minimum of the auxiliary loss $\alpha E\sum_i f_iP_i$ under the constraint $\sum_i f_i=1$ and show it corresponds to uniform routing; simulate the collapse (biased initialization of the router) without then with the loss.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: at router equilibrium, $P_i=f_i$; minimize $E\sum f_i^2$ under $\sum f_i=1$ → Lagrange → uniform $f_i=1/E$; without the loss, the winning expert attracts tokens (reinforced feedback) and specialization degenerates. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **Guided SFT.** Fine-tune a small instructed model (1-3B) on 500 (question, answer) pairs from your domain: strict template, masked labels (code of ch. 4), 2-3 epochs; measure the effect of a wrong template at test time (a spectacular drop to witness once and for all).
7.  **DPO on paper.** Derive the closed form $\pi^\star$ of the KL-penalized problem (classical calculus of variations), then the DPO loss by re-injecting into Bradley-Terry; check the gradient: it increases the log-ratio margin of the preferred responses.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: follow the proof of thm 5.2 step by step — the key argument is that $\mathcal{J}=-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}e^{r/\beta}/Z)+\beta\log Z$; then $Z(x)$ disappears in the difference $r^+-r^-$. The gradient pushes $\log\pi(y^+)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^+)$ up and the $y^-$ down, modulated by $\sigma(-\hat r)$ (hard pairs first). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
8.  **Toy GRPO.** On a verifiable task (binary arithmetic), train a mini-model with GRPO (group of 8 responses); plot accuracy and response length — observe the emergence of longer "reasoning"; compare gradient variance with/without normalization by the group standard deviation.
9.  **Speculative, on paper.** Write out completely the proof of thm 6.3 in the case $\gamma=2$, then estimate the expected latency gain if $q=p$ on 80% of the mass but diverges on the rest.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: accept token 1 (probability $\sum_y\min(q,p)$), then the second conditionally; the expected number of accepted tokens per round is $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ (geometric) with $\alpha\approx0.8$ → \~5 tokens/forward; gain bounded by $\gamma$ and by the small/large model cost ratio. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
10. **RAG vs context length.** Query an LLM with 4k/32k/128k of context over a corpus: does the "lost in the middle" effect appear? Compare with RAG; discuss the trade-offs (cost, faithfulness, indexing overhead).
11. **Watermark.** With $\gamma=0.5$ and $T=400$ tokens, compute $z$ for a text carrying 230 green tokens; threshold at 5%; how many tokens are needed to detect a +5% green bias?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: $z=(230-200)/10 = 3$ → p ≈ 0.1%: rejected (marked); for a small bias $\varepsilon$, the expectation of $z$ grows like $\varepsilon\sqrt{T/\gamma(1-\gamma)}$ → one needs $T\sim (1.96/\varepsilon)^2\gamma(1-\gamma)$; with $\varepsilon=0.05$, \~770 tokens — hence the difficulty on short texts. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
12. **Agent project.** Extend the final lab: an agent that chooses *between* vector retrieval and a graph query depending on the question type (relational or factual) — measure the improvement and the extra cost.
